questions.stem: Many small marsupials forage at night and shelter in burrows or hollows during the day. This is a response to:
options: a seasonal cycle in rainfall and day length
a tidal cycle in water and salinity levels
a fire cycle in vegetation and shelter
a diurnal cycle in light and temperature
questions.explanation: Diurnal cycles are the daily changes in light and temperature caused by Earth's rotation. Nocturnal activity avoids daytime heat and predators. Seasonal cycles operate over a year, not a day.

questions.stem: Why do deciduous trees and many alpine plants in Tasmania grow mainly in spring and summer?
options: Lower light in summer protects leaves from damage, so plants grow faster
Longer days and warmer temperatures increase photosynthesis and growth
Shorter days and colder temperatures increase photosynthesis and growth
Higher snowfall in summer supplies the extra water needed for growth
questions.explanation: Seasonal changes in day length and temperature control the rate of photosynthesis and growth. In winter, short days, low temperatures and snow cover limit growth, especially at high altitude.

questions.stem: In a shallow freshwater pond, dissolved oxygen is usually highest in the late afternoon and lowest just before dawn. Why?
options: Photosynthesis adds oxygen during daylight, while respiration uses it all night
Respiration adds oxygen during daylight, while photosynthesis uses it all night
Cold water at dawn holds much less oxygen than warm water in the afternoon
Animals use oxygen only during the day and release it again during the night
questions.explanation: During the day, producers release oxygen faster than organisms use it. At night photosynthesis stops but respiration continues, so oxygen falls until sunrise. Cold water actually holds more dissolved oxygen, not less.

questions.stem: A rock pool high on the shore is cut off from the sea for several hours on a hot day at low tide. Which changes are most likely in the pool?
options: Water temperature falls and salinity drops as the pool water evaporates
Water temperature and salinity both stay the same as the open sea
Dissolved oxygen rises steadily because warm water holds more oxygen
Water temperature and salinity rise as the water warms and evaporates
questions.explanation: Isolated from the sea, the small volume of water heats up and evaporation concentrates the salt. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, so oxygen tends to fall, especially if the pool stays cut off overnight.

questions.stem: Barnacles live higher on a rocky shore than kelp, which grows only at and below the low-tide mark. The best explanation for this zonation is that:
options: barnacles tolerate drying out and heat during low tide, while kelp cannot
kelp tolerates drying out and heat during low tide better than barnacles
kelp needs less sunlight, so it must live higher up on the rocky shore
barnacles need constant submersion, so they live where the tide never leaves
questions.explanation: Organisms high on the shore are exposed for longer at low tide, so they must tolerate desiccation, temperature swings and salinity changes. Kelp is submerged almost all the time, so it lives low on the shore where exposure is shortest.

questions.stem: Which factor changes the most for organisms in the intertidal zone over a tidal cycle?
options: Water availability, as they are covered and uncovered by the tide
Day length, as the incoming tide shortens the hours of sunlight each day
Air pressure, as the tide pushes the air above the shore upward
Gravity, as the tide changes the weight of animals on the rocks
questions.explanation: Intertidal organisms are submerged at high tide and exposed to air at low tide, changing water availability, temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen and light. The tide does not change day length or gravity for these organisms.

questions.stem: During an El Nino event, eastern Australia typically experiences:
options: increased rainfall, cooler days and a much greater risk of flooding
increased rainfall, higher temperatures and fewer heatwaves
reduced rainfall, cooler days and a lower bushfire risk
reduced rainfall, higher temperatures and greater bushfire risk
questions.explanation: El Nino is linked to below-average rainfall over much of eastern Australia, warmer temperatures, more heatwaves and higher bushfire risk. Increased rainfall and flooding are associated with La Nina.

questions.stem: Which change in the Pacific is a general feature of an El Nino event?
options: Trade winds stay the same while the ocean near Australia warms sharply
Trade winds weaken and warmer water spreads to the central and eastern Pacific
Trade winds strengthen and warm water piles up in the western Pacific near Australia
Trade winds reverse and cold water spreads westward to the coast of Australia
questions.explanation: In El Nino the easterly trade winds weaken, so warm surface water spreads east and cloud and rainfall shift away from Australia. Stronger trade winds piling warm water near Australia describes La Nina.

questions.stem: A farmer in eastern Australia hears that a La Nina event has been declared. Which outcome should she plan for?
options: No change in rainfall, as La Nina affects only the eastern Pacific Ocean
Above-average rainfall, with a higher chance of waterlogging and flooding
Below-average rainfall, with a much higher chance of drought and crop failure
Hotter, drier conditions, with a much higher risk of summer bushfires
questions.explanation: La Nina typically brings increased rainfall to much of eastern Australia, raising the risk of flooding and waterlogged soils. Drought and higher bushfire risk are associated with El Nino.

questions.stem: A sustained strongly negative Southern Oscillation Index over several months, together with warming of the central Pacific, indicates:
options: a La Nina event, with drier conditions likely over eastern Australia
an El Nino event, with drier conditions likely over eastern Australia
a La Nina event, with wetter conditions likely over eastern Australia
an El Nino event, with wetter conditions likely over eastern Australia
questions.explanation: Sustained negative SOI values, along with a warming central and eastern Pacific, are characteristic of El Nino, which tends to reduce rainfall over eastern Australia. Sustained positive values indicate La Nina.

questions.stem: Many eucalypts resprout from epicormic buds under their bark after a bushfire. This adaptation allows them to:
options: release seeds only in years when there has been no fire in the forest
move their roots deeper so that the next fire cannot reach their buds
regrow leaves quickly from the trunk and branches after the canopy is burnt
avoid catching fire because the buds produce chemicals that stop the flames spreading
questions.explanation: Epicormic buds are protected under thick bark and sprout after fire, letting the tree rebuild its canopy quickly. Eucalypts are flammable; their adaptations help them recover from fire rather than avoid burning.

questions.stem: A Tasmanian wet eucalypt forest has a rainforest understorey. If it remains unburnt for several hundred years, the most likely change is that:
options: the forest turns into grassland because there are no fires to stop it
the eucalypts die without regenerating and rainforest species take over
the eucalypts regenerate more strongly because fire is no longer present
the rainforest species die out because they need regular fire to survive
questions.explanation: Tall wet eucalypts need fire to open the canopy and prepare a seedbed for their seedlings. Without fire, shade-tolerant rainforest trees replace them over centuries. Rainforest species are fire-sensitive, not fire-dependent.

questions.stem: Why are Tasmanian rainforest conifers such as pencil pine and King Billy pine especially threatened by bushfire?
options: They grow only in grassland, where fires are hotter than in any other ecosystem
They are very fire-sensitive and regenerate poorly, so one fire can kill whole stands
They need frequent fire to open their cones, so fewer fires stop their regeneration entirely
They resprout after fire so quickly that they outcompete the native grasses
questions.explanation: These conifers are very fire-sensitive, grow slowly and seed only infrequently, so a single fire can destroy stands that took centuries to establish, and burnt stands may not recover. They rely on long fire-free intervals, not frequent fire.

questions.stem: How do Antarctic ice cores record past atmospheric composition?
options: The colour of each ice layer shows how much carbon dioxide was in the air
Fossils of plants frozen in the ice show which gases they absorbed in life
Ice melts faster when greenhouse gas levels rise, so the thickness of each layer shows them
Tiny air bubbles trapped as snow compacts into ice preserve samples of past air
questions.explanation: As snow accumulates and compresses into ice, it traps bubbles of air that can be analysed for carbon dioxide and methane. Deep Antarctic cores give records reaching back about 800 000 years.

questions.stem: Ice core records show that over the last 800 000 years, carbon dioxide concentration:
options: rose and fell with glacial and interglacial periods, and is now far above that natural range
stayed almost constant until the last century, so past climates were all the same as today's
was always higher than today, and has steadily fallen since the end of the last ice age
rose and fell with glacial periods, and is now at the lowest level in the whole record
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide varied roughly between 180 and 280 ppm, low in glacial and high in interglacial periods. Since industrialisation it has risen far above that range.

questions.stem: Where is the Kennaook/Cape Grim Baseline Air Pollution Station, and what makes its air valuable for monitoring?
options: North-east Tasmania, where air from mainland Australia arrives over Bass Strait each day
North-west Tasmania, where winds off the Southern Ocean bring air largely free of local pollution
South-east Tasmania, where air from Hobart lets scientists measure the city's pollution directly
Central Tasmania, where the high altitude means air is not affected by the ocean at all
questions.explanation: Cape Grim is at the north-west tip of Tasmania. When winds blow from the south-west, the air has crossed thousands of kilometres of Southern Ocean, so it represents clean background (baseline) air. It is run by the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO and began measuring in 1976.

questions.stem: The seasonal rise and fall in carbon dioxide recorded at Mauna Loa in Hawaii is much larger than at Cape Grim in Tasmania. The best explanation is that:
options: Cape Grim measures only ocean air, which contains no carbon dioxide at any time of the year
Mauna Loa is an active volcano, so its eruptions each summer add a large seasonal pulse of carbon dioxide
the Northern Hemisphere has far more land vegetation, whose seasonal growth takes up and releases more CO2
the Southern Hemisphere has far more land vegetation, which absorbs CO2 evenly throughout the year
questions.explanation: Most of Earth's land and forests are in the Northern Hemisphere, so northern spring and summer growth draws down CO2 strongly and autumn decay releases it. The ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere has a much smaller seasonal cycle. Both stations show the same long-term upward trend.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Mauna Loa and Cape Grim records is the strongest evidence of human influence on the atmosphere?
options: A seasonal rise and fall in carbon dioxide concentration that repeats every year
A difference in carbon dioxide concentration between the two stations in each month
A sharp fall in carbon dioxide concentration during each El Nino event recorded
A steady year-on-year rise in carbon dioxide concentration since measurements began
questions.explanation: The long-term upward trend, matching rising fossil fuel use, shows carbon dioxide accumulating in the atmosphere. The seasonal cycle is natural, caused by plant growth and decay.

questions.stem: How can corals provide evidence of past climate?
options: They grow only in years with high rainfall, so missing bands show past droughts
They change colour permanently each time sea level rises, recording past sea levels
They lay down seasonal bands of calcium carbonate whose chemistry reflects water temperature
They trap air bubbles inside their skeletons that record past carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Coral skeletons grow in annual layers, and their density and chemical composition (such as oxygen isotopes) vary with sea temperature, giving a year-by-year record. Air bubble records come from ice cores, not corals.

questions.stem: Tree-ring records from long-lived Huon pine on Mount Read in western Tasmania have been used to reconstruct past temperatures. What do wider rings generally indicate?
options: Years with more favourable growing conditions, such as warmer summers
Years when the tree was damaged by fire and grew no new wood at all
Years with less favourable conditions, so the tree stored extra wood
Years with heavy snow, when the tree grew only during the winter
questions.explanation: Each ring is one year's growth, and its width reflects how favourable conditions were. For high-altitude trees such as those on Mount Read, summer temperature is a strong control, so ring widths track past temperatures over thousands of years.

questions.stem: Which type of evidence from a lake sediment core is most useful for reconstructing past vegetation and climate?
options: Pollen grains preserved in each layer of sediment
Air bubbles trapped between the grains of sediment
Annual growth rings formed in the sediment by trees
Calcium carbonate bands laid down by living coral
questions.explanation: Pollen settles into lake sediments and is preserved layer by layer, showing which plants grew nearby and hence the past climate. Air bubbles are an ice core method, and coral bands come from reefs.

questions.stem: An ancient beach, with rounded pebbles and shells, is found several metres above present high-tide level along a coastline. This is best interpreted as evidence that:
options: glaciers carried the beach inland and up from the present shore
relative sea level was once higher, or the land has since risen
relative sea level has always been the same as it is today
the beach was built by wind carrying pebbles uphill from the sea
questions.explanation: Raised beaches mark former shorelines left above today's sea level, either because sea level was higher in the past or because the land has been uplifted, for example as it rebounded after ice melted. Wind cannot move rounded pebbles and shell beds uphill in this way.

questions.stem: Cirques, U-shaped valleys and moraines in Tasmania's Central Highlands are evidence that:
options: volcanoes erupted across the Central Highlands in recent times
rivers in Tasmania once flowed much faster than they do now
glaciers covered parts of Tasmania during past cold periods
sea level was once higher than the Central Highlands today
questions.explanation: These landforms are made by moving ice: cirques are carved basins, U-shaped valleys are glacial troughs and moraines are ridges of debris dropped by glaciers. They show that Tasmania's highlands were glaciated during past ice ages.

questions.stem: Ozone depletion over Antarctica is caused mainly by:
options: methane from livestock rising into the stratosphere and absorbing the ozone
sulfur dioxide from volcanoes that converts ozone into acid rain over the ice
chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other ozone-depleting chemicals in the stratosphere
carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels reacting with ozone in the lower troposphere
questions.explanation: Chlorine and bromine released from CFCs and halons break down ozone in the stratosphere, especially in the Antarctic spring. Carbon dioxide drives the enhanced greenhouse effect but is not the main cause of ozone depletion.

questions.stem: Why is stratospheric ozone depletion a concern for ecosystems and people?
options: Less oxygen reaches the surface, so organisms cannot respire as efficiently
Less visible light reaches the surface, so photosynthesis stops in winter
More ultraviolet radiation reaches the surface, damaging DNA in living things
More infrared radiation is trapped, so ozone depletion is the main cause of warming
questions.explanation: The ozone layer absorbs much of the Sun's harmful UV-B radiation. Thinner ozone lets more UV reach the surface, increasing skin cancer risk and damaging plants and plankton. Ozone depletion and global warming are different problems.

questions.stem: How does rising atmospheric carbon dioxide lead to ocean acidification?
options: CO2 dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid, lowering the ocean's pH
CO2 warms the ocean surface, and warmer water always has a higher pH
CO2 reacts with dissolved salt to form hydrochloric acid in the upper ocean layer
CO2 kills plankton, and their decaying bodies raise the ocean's pH
questions.explanation: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, releasing hydrogen ions and lowering pH. Ocean surface pH has fallen by about 0.1 since pre-industrial times, which is a substantial increase in acidity.

questions.stem: Why does ocean acidification threaten shell-building organisms such as oysters and some plankton?
options: More carbonate ions are available, making their shells grow too thick to function
Acidic water always contains less dissolved oxygen, so shell-building animals suffocate
Acidic water is colder, which stops shell-building animals from feeding at all
Fewer carbonate ions are available, making it harder to build calcium carbonate shells
questions.explanation: The extra hydrogen ions combine with carbonate ions, reducing the carbonate that organisms need to make calcium carbonate shells and skeletons. In more acidic water existing shells can also begin to dissolve.

questions.stem: Coral bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel their zooxanthellae. Which combination of conditions can trigger bleaching?
options: Unusually clear water, lower turbidity or a rise in the number of fish
Unusually high water temperature, lower pH or a sudden drop in salinity
Unusually low light levels, a higher pH or a sharp rise in dissolved oxygen
Unusually cool water temperature, more nutrients or stronger currents
questions.explanation: Marine heatwaves are the main cause of mass bleaching, but acidification and freshwater floods lowering salinity also stress corals. Without the algae, corals lose most of their food supply and may die if conditions do not recover.

questions.stem: What are the two main causes of global sea level rise as the climate warms?
options: Increased evaporation from oceans and sinking of the sea floor
Thermal expansion of seawater and melting of land-based ice
Melting of floating sea ice and increased rainfall over oceans
Thermal contraction of seawater and melting of floating sea ice
questions.explanation: Water expands as it warms, and meltwater from glaciers and ice sheets on land adds water to the oceans. Floating sea ice already displaces its own mass of water, so its melting adds very little to sea level.

questions.stem: A low-lying coastal town notices more frequent flooding during storms, even though storm strength has not changed. The most likely climate-related explanation is:
options: lower sea level exposes more of the beach, allowing waves to reach the town
colder oceans make storm surges heavier, so they push further inland
melting sea ice in the Arctic directly raises the tide level near the town
higher sea level raises the base on which storm surges and high tides build
questions.explanation: With a higher mean sea level, the same storm surge and tide reach further inland, increasing coastal flooding and erosion. Floating sea ice melt adds very little to sea level.

questions.stem: The East Australian Current has extended further south, bringing warmer water down Tasmania's east coast. Which ecological change has been linked to this?
options: Giant kelp forests expanding rapidly because warmer water has more nutrients
Cold-water fish species moving north along the east coast to warmer water
Seagrass beds disappearing because the warm current has lowered the salinity
The long-spined sea urchin spreading south and grazing kelp beds into barrens
questions.explanation: Larvae carried south by the strengthened current allowed the long-spined sea urchin to establish in eastern Tasmania, where its grazing creates barrens stripped of kelp. Warm water is generally low in nutrients, and kelp forests have declined, not expanded.

questions.stem: Climate scientists expect global warming to change extreme weather by:
options: decreasing the frequency of all extreme events, because the whole climate becomes milder
increasing only the number of cold snaps, because warming slows ocean currents
ending droughts, because warmer air always brings more rain to every region
increasing the frequency and intensity of events such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall
questions.explanation: A warmer atmosphere brings more frequent and intense heatwaves, and because warm air holds more moisture, heavier rainfall events too. Some regions also face more severe droughts, so warming does not end drought everywhere.

questions.stem: Over several decades, a species of fish is found further south along the Australian coast than before. This is best explained as:
options: a change in species distribution as warmer conditions extend its suitable habitat
a change in species distribution because cold southern water now extends further north
an adaptation that each fish developed during its own lifetime to cope with heat
a change in phenology, as the fish now breeds earlier in the year than before
questions.explanation: As waters warm, conditions within a species' tolerance range shift towards the poles, so its distribution moves south in the Southern Hemisphere. Phenology refers to the timing of events such as breeding, not to where species live.

questions.stem: A bird times its breeding so chicks hatch when caterpillars are most abundant. With warmer springs, the caterpillars now emerge two weeks earlier, but the birds still breed at the same time. The most likely consequence is:
options: the caterpillars will be forced to change their timing back to the old dates
loss of synchrony, so fewer chicks are fed well and breeding success falls
better breeding success, because the caterpillars are larger when chicks hatch
no effect, because the birds will switch to eating nectar instead of insects
questions.explanation: If food peaks before chicks hatch, the parents cannot find enough food at the critical time, so chick survival drops. This mismatch in the timing of biological events (phenology) is a documented effect of climate change.

questions.stem: Why is climate change expected to make agricultural food production less reliable?
options: More stable weather patterns encourage pests to spread to new areas each year
More variable rainfall, more droughts and heat stress reduce yields unpredictably
Higher carbon dioxide stops photosynthesis in crops, so yields always fall to zero
Lower temperatures shorten the growing season for all crops in every region
questions.explanation: Changes in rainfall timing and amount, more frequent droughts, floods and heatwaves, and shifting pest ranges make yields harder to predict. Higher carbon dioxide does not stop photosynthesis.

questions.stem: The enhanced greenhouse effect refers to:
options: cooling caused by ozone depletion letting more heat escape to space
warming caused by the Sun becoming brighter over the last century
extra warming caused by human additions of greenhouse gases to the atmosphere
natural warming that keeps Earth's average surface temperature suitable for all life
questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the additional warming from human emissions of gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, leading to climate change.
